trace.topic: The Rise of the “N=1” App: When Building It Yourself Really Beats Buying It.
trace.goal: Explain when custom internal AI software is the right choice.
expected_facts: The answer should argue that some AI-native workflows are now cheap enough to build internally.
It should explain that the build-vs-buy line has shifted for narrow, custom workflows.
It should caution that not every internal use case deserves custom software.
rubric_must_haves: Takes a position on when building makes sense.
Explains why AI changes the economics.
Keeps the advice grounded in operator tradeoffs.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that AI lowers the cost of building narrow internal tools, which makes custom software a smarter choice in some cases than it used to be. The best candidates are high-value workflows with very specific requirements that off-the-shelf tools handle poorly. The lesson is not to build everything, but to recognize when a tailored app now has unusually high leverage.

The Rise of the “N=1” App:

When Building It Yourself Really Beats Buying It

At some point this year you’ll find yourself staring down a workflow problem so gnawingly painful that buying another tool seems like admitting defeat. So many tools. But then you think … what if I could just make something myself? And that’s when you become a founder again—albeit temporarily, without the equity upside.

Here’s my confession: At SaaStr, I’ve been building my own apps since January. Not because I’m trying to overthrow Salesforce (though I do have a Salesforce replacement on deck). But because most enterprise software still doesn’t work the way founders want it to. We’re all running the same old playbook built decades ago, optimized around human teams doing repetitive

retrieval_hits.text:
1. The Build vs. Buy Decision Isn’t Binary
A common mistake companies make is thinking they need to either build everything from scratch or rely entirely on third-party APIs. The reality is more nuanced:
Start with clear use cases
: Don’t implement AI just because it’s trendy. Dialpad began with specific problems they wanted to solve around conversation intelligence.
Understand the trade-offs
: Real-time processing has different cost, throughput, and risk profiles compared to batch processing. Make this decision early.
Consider a hybrid approach
: You can start with third-party APIs while building your data foundation, then gradually move to custom solutions as you scale.

The Future May Not Be Here, But If Not, It’s Close
Here’s the perspective that keeps me sleeping at night with my spend
Traditional approach for a commercial app:
Hire development team: $50,000-150,000
Timeline: 3-6 months
Managing contractors, QA, deployment
Doesn’t really work the way you wanted
Still need technical co-founder or CTO
My ideation-to-commercial experiment:
Timeline: 30-45 days
Cost: $8,000-$10,000 (even worst case)
Full control and understanding of every line
Learning while building
Can iterate and pivot instantly
If this works, it’s a 10x improvement in cost and speed. The Hidden Costs Everyone Ignores
When you see that $607.70 charge for the first few days, you’re not just paying for compute. You’re paying for:
Compressed Learning Cycles
Instead of spending weeks reading documentation
Instead of trial-and-error debugging sessions
Instead of architectural mistakes that cost days to fix
Premium Development Experience
Instant code reviews and suggestions
Architecture guidance from a AI
Debugging partner that never gets tired
Opportunity Cost Mitigation
Shipping in hours instead of days
Getting to market faster — possibly. Possibly. Learning while building instead of building while learning
The Scenarios You Should Budget For
Based on my experience and others I’ve talked to, there are a lot of play apps you can build for the base $20-$25 a month. But you can’t go that far.

Software is always cheaper to buy than to build

So that's just an excuse

So I’ve spent over 200 hours vibe coding the last 100 or so days. And I really don’t have a spare 200 hours. Why? One reason was to learn. But not really. The real reason was to build things I needed to build, I wanted to build, that … I just couldn’t get built otherwise. One app that I’d been waiting 10 years to build. Build those ones. The ones you want to will into existence, but just can’t find the help. The ones you need to build, but are too niche to excite most developers. Build the app you’ve been yearning to build. That’s what will push you through the learning curve, the screenshots, the iterates, the 100s of releases, the rough patches, the regressions, and more.
